doc.title: Al Grey interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995

title: Basie as 'Chief' and Grey becoming featured soloist
summary: Basie becomes like a father; the band calls him 'Chief.' Grey gets featured and Henry Coker and Benny Powell leave.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Tell us about that name, when you called him “Chief.”

Yeah, well, after that he became like my father, everybody called him “Chief.” Not Count Basie or Count or nothing. It was Chief. And anybody, everyone in that band, it was “Chief,” not Count Basie or Basie. But before I went into the band it was always “Count Basie” see. And so Basie then would say that you’ve got a place here. So we come back to New York, and they wrote up so much music for me until one day Basie had to come to me and say that I’m getting static from the other trombone players, and I’m going to have to take some of these numbers and put them in a shuffle here and pass them out to Henry Coker and Benny Powell, because they’re not — he really took a liking to me and so I became his featured star, you understand? And then, it was Sonny Payne and then Joe Williams, okay? So from this he passed out these different tunes for solos, but it got to the place he still, that he did call these numbers. And so Henry Coker became upset about this, because he had been there, and so he decided to leave the band and he went with Ray Charles. And this was how it happened, see, because he wasn’t getting enough to play. And then Benny Powell left and went with Merv Griffin show, you see, because they said that here I just come in and took over. What about this monster, you know? But it wasn’t meant like that, it was just that we didn’t get enough playing time. You’ve got to get some playing time if you want to be out in this business, see? And so if it’s meant that you have to play for a show that’s come on, play for Ella Fitzgerald, play for Frank Sinatra, there’s no room to give everybody a solo. So but you do get a chance to do a solo when you play a dance. But then that’s when you’re not noticed that much, because they’re there to dance and they are there to talk to their friends. And this is a completely different type of interview here, I must tell you that, but this is the way it was.
